articles.title: ECB chair Richard Thompson 'extremely disappointed' at England cricket off-field incidents
articles.summary: Brydon Carse episode outside a Derby nightclub latest off-field issue for England to manage after Harry Brook being punched by a bouncer, Ben Duckett video in Noosa and Gus Atkinson and Ben Stokes breaking curfew earlier this summer; Joe Root "hacked off" with team's "stupid mistakes"
articles.body:
Fast bowler Brydon Carse was dropped for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's as the Cricket Regulator examines an incident outside a Derby nightclub last weekend.

The Carse situation follows Harry Brook being punched by a bouncer in New Zealand last year, Ben Duckett videoed seemingly drunk in Noosa during The Ashes, and Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson breaking curfew to attend a London nightspot this summer.

New captain Joe Root, who has taken over from the retired Stokes, said he was "hacked off" by England continuing to make "stupid mistakes" when speaking to the media earlier this week.

'Every player has to understand responsibility of playing for England'

Thompson said to Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton on Friday morning: "I don't think anyone could have summed it up better than Joe [Root] did this week.

"When you play for your country, you are judged by a far higher standard. What comes with wearing the three lions comes with respect, responsibility and pride.

"Unless you live and breathe those three qualities, there's a problem. I think every player, and Joe articulated this brilliantly, has to understand the responsibility that comes with playing for England."

Speaking about the Carse story at Lord's on Thursday, Sky Sports pundit and former England seamer Stuart Broad said: "Carse is in a very worrying situation because Root is now in charge. It's a fresh page. Joe can say, 'this is my team, this is what we are doing'.

"When you are getting reprimanded by the Cricket Regulator or the ECB, you don't know who that is, but when Root says, 'I expect this from you and if you don't deliver that we have a problem', then you are not crossing Root.

"That is the strong position Root is in after what he has said to the group - players will start to behave.

"I thought what Root said in the press conference was very strong and what an opportunity for him to say, 'this is my team and we will do it my way'."

Thompson: England wanted to be 'measured' after Ashes

Root will work alongside new Test coach Stephen Fleming moving forward with the latter succeeding fellow New Zealander Brendon McCullum in the role.

Fleming's first assignment will be a three-match series in South Africa over the winter, with Marcus Trescothick in interim charge against Pakistan.

McCullum was axed following the 2-1 home defeat to New Zealand in June, having presided over seven defeats and just two wins in England's previous nine Tests.

Asked why change did not come after the error-strewn 4-1 Ashes thrashing in Australia this winter, Thompson added: "We all wanted to be very considered.

"When you lose 4-1, the expectation is that heads will roll. That's what's always happened before. The reality is when you lose an Ashes, a number of people lose their jobs.

"You learn nothing from it. You never get the chance to learn what those lessons were, and you never get to understand what those lessons are and put them right.

"Within days of the Ashes finishing, we were also going into a Sri Lanka white-ball tour and an important T20 World Cup with the same coaching group and players.

"That's the reality of modern cricket; being swift is hard when you are back-to-back with tournaments.

"The reality was we wanted to be measured. We felt that there were lessons that could and should have been learned."

articles.title: Sarah Taylor: England fielding coach says role has been 'strange' but 'amazing' and enjoying working with Jamie Smith
articles.summary: Sarah Taylor first woman to coach an England men's side in a major sport; former wicketkeeper played 226 internationals for England women between 2006-2019; Taylor enjoying watching wicketkeepers standing up to the seam bowlers in Test cricket and says it allows them to show their skills
articles.body:
Former England women's player Taylor, regarded as one of the best wicketkeepers the game has seen, began her role with the senior men's side team this summer, following coaching stints with England Lions, Sussex and in The Hundred.

The 37-year-old is the first woman to coach an England men's side in a major sport.

Speaking to Sky Sports Cricket's Ian Ward prior to day two of the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's, Taylor said of her job: "It is a bit strange but what's brilliant about these guys is that they just call me coach.

"That's exactly what you want. I am entering their space so I have to respect their space. I have genuinely loved it, felt so welcome.

"It has been a normal transition into the Lions set-up and then this set-up. The boys have been amazing and I cannot complain at all."

'Smith is a project and knows what he needs to do'

Smith's glovework has been largely immaculate this summer, with the Surrey man often asked to move up to the stumps to the seamers, a trend in the global game and one Australia and New Zealand have deployed against England in recent series.

Taylor said of the England wicketkeeper: "Jamie has been very clear on what he wants to achieve and where he wants to go with his keeping. He is a project and he knows what he needs to do.

"It is just little tinkering changes here and there. His stood-up stuff has definitely improved and his movement as well.

"We get on extremely well and clicked straightaway, which is a blessing as a coach. I have loved it, it has been an absolute dream."

On wicketkeepers coming up to the stumps more generally, Taylor added: "A few years ago the wicketkeeper standing up was a punch to a bowler's ego, whereas now it is seen as a real positive.

"You are trying to enhance those bowlers' skills, especially when the ball is nipping around and the wicket is helpful for that.

"Wicketkeepers have to get better at that, especially against the speed they are facing.

"Ultimately, that's what Jamie has been working extremely hard on - staying a lot more still, especially with the moving ball.

"Watching some of the wicketkeepers, they are really showing their true skill that they weren't able to show as much before.

articles.title: Marnus Labuschagne: Ricky Ponting says Australia batter's place in Test team 'almost untenable' after lean run of form
articles.summary: Ricky Ponting expects batting changes when Australia tour South Africa -  "I don't think we are going to get any worse or lose anything and may just unearth a really good talent"; Ponting also speaks on Mike Hussey being linked with England batting coach role and Century Cricket project
articles.body:
No 3 batter Labuschagne made scores of one, 31 and four during the recent 1-1 series draw at home to Bangladesh and has not registered a Test century in 43 innings.

The 32-year-old, hoping to be included in the squad for the three-Test series in South Africa from October 9, last hit a ton in the Manchester Ashes Test against England in 2023.

Ponting - speaking to Sky Sports News in his role as ambassador, investor and global advisor for Century Cricket, a coaching and talent ID centre launching in Manhattan, New York - had already noted Labuschagne's troubles scoring off the back foot while analysing the Bangladesh series for Australian broadcaster Channel 7 .

The 51-year-old said of Australia: "This has been a very dominant side for a long period of time but I think they have been carrying few guys through the last couple of years.

"I think it is inevitable that change is made going to South Africa - Labuschagne's spot in the side is almost untenable, so they have to look at someone at No 3.

"Eventually they will also want Travis Head back at No 5 rather than opening, so that could present a chance for a youngster to come in and open the batting.

"It won't be easy against that South Africa attack but we have got to the point where we have to try something. I don't think we are going to get any worse or lose anything and may just unearth a really good talent as well."

'England have talent to serve it up to Australia'

There has been change for England's Test side this summer.

Captain Ben Stokes quit international cricket and Brendon McCullum was sacked as head coach after a run of seven defeats and just two wins in his final 10 matches in charge, including an error-strewn 4-1 Ashes drubbing over the winter.

Joe Root has replaced Stokes and began his second stint as skipper with a series win over Pakistan, while former New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming has been named McCullum's replacement and will take over properly ahead of the winter tour of South Africa.

Ponting, speaking before England completed victory over Pakistan at Lord's , said: "I wasn't surprised to see changes after The Ashes, although the way it came around was maybe a bit different than what I thought.

"With Joe back as captain and a different personality altogether in Fleming, there is no doubt the talent is there to really serve it up to the Australians in the next Ashes."

'Hussey could slip back into England role'

Ex-Australia batter Mike Hussey has been linked with the position of England batting coach, having performed that role for IPL team Chennai Super Kings while Fleming was head coach, but Ponting feels other job opportunities could soon come his former team-mate's way.

Hussey, who played 79 Tests, 185 one-day internationals and 38 T20 internationals for his country between 2005 and 2013, previously served as England's batting consultant during their T20 World Cup triumph in Australia in 2022.

Ponting said: "I saw Mike Hussey last week and said, 'if you take that job I will never speak to you again!' I think I have scared him off!

"I am not sure what he is going to do. I believe there might be a job in the pipeline for him around the Australian team, so I am not sure of his status.

"I also read a report he might be the next head coach of Chennai Super Kings, which could rule him out of everything anyway.

"At the end of the day, we are all coaches and in it to do whatever we can do. He has done [the England job] before and could easily slip back into that role again."

Ponting eager to grow cricket in the USA

On his role with Century Cricket, Ponting - head coach of Punjab Kings in the IPL and Washington Freedom in the US-based Major League Cricket - added: "To be involved with a platform like this that I can use as a coaching and talent-identification tool and to get down to growing the game in the US is the major reason I am involved.

"Cricket hasn't grown as rapidly as I would have thought in the US, but with what we have been able to create, it will allow people of all ages to sample what the game is all about skill-wise.

"It's a platform like I've never seen before. The technology is second to none and I can't wait to watch."

Training can be pre-set for particular deliveries, bowlers and match scenarios, with Century Cricket's global CEO Chris Millard adding: "It really is a global platform that can change cricket for the better.

"People can face a Jasprit Bumrah or a Moeen Ali in whatever setting they want. We have the data to pull that off and if we are able to scale that globally we will be starting the future of cricket."

articles.title: Ben Stokes: Former England Test captain signs for Adelaide Strikers in Big Bash League
articles.summary: Former England cricketer Ben Stokes will return to the Big Bash League this winter, joining the Adelaide Strikers for his first appearance in the franchise tournament since the 2014-15 season; Stokes retired from international cricket in June
articles.body:
Stokes will play in the franchise competition this winter after penning a one-year deal with the side following his retirement from international cricket.

It marks his return to the BBL for the first time in 12 years. He last played during the 2014-15 season for the Melbourne Renegades.

Stokes stunned the cricketing world when he announced his decision to step down as England's Test captain and retire from international cricket midway through his side's third Test against New Zealand in June.

The shock announcement came during the afternoon session on the fourth day of the series decider at Trent Bridge, with Stokes bowling when the news broke. He responded by taking a wicket with the very next ball.

His decision came after he was left out of the second Test against New Zealand following an investigation into an incident at a London nightclub.

He returned for the third Test, during which he made the decision to step down.

On making the decision to play in the BBL, Stokes said: "I'm really excited to be joining the Adelaide Strikers for BBL|16.

"I've always enjoyed playing in Australia, and when the opportunity came up to join the Strikers it was one I couldn't pass up.

"Adelaide Oval is an incredible place to play cricket, the Big Bash is a fantastic competition and the Strikers have an exciting group, so I'm looking forward to meeting the players, getting stuck in and contributing to a successful season.

"I can't wait to get started, create some special memories with the group and give Strikers fans plenty to cheer about."

Adelaide Strikers head coach Tim Paine said: "Ben is one of the greatest all-rounders the game has seen, a proven match-winner and a competitor who thrives under pressure.

"We're thrilled to have a player of his ability join our squad and can't wait to see him put on a show in BBL|16.

"Our fans have watched him produce some of the most memorable moments over the past decade, and now they'll have the chance to see him in Strikers blue.

"Adelaide Oval is the best place in the world to play and watch cricket, so we're looking forward to seeing our members and fans flock through the gates to watch him in action."

articles.title: Scott Kuggeleijn: Hampshire confirm New Zealand all-rounder will not feature for club after criticism over signing
articles.summary: Scott Kuggeleijn represented New Zealand in all three formats and signed for Hampshire for the rest of the County Championship season; Hampshire released a statement to confirm he would not play, following widespread criticism about his arrival
articles.body:
Kuggeleijn was charged with sexual violation by rape and indecent assault in 2015, having pleaded not guilty. He was later acquitted after a second trial, following a hung jury in the first trial.

Hampshire listed Kuggeleijn in their squad for their Rothesay County Championship match against Warwickshire on Tuesday, beginning Wednesday, then confirmed later that day they had signed the 34-year-old for the final four matches of the season.

The signing immediately received a negative reaction on social media, with comments describing the moving as "disgusting" and "a new low for the club", leading to Hampshire announcing on Wednesday that he would not play.

"Having reflected and listened to feedback from our staff and supporters, Hampshire Cricket can confirm that Scott Kuggeleijn will not represent the club," a statement read.

"We value the passion of our fanbase and thank everyone who took the time to share their views. Our focus now turns to supporting the team through the final four County Championship fixtures of the season.

"We encourage everyone to unite behind the team as we enter a crucial stage of the campaign."

Kuggeleijn has represented New Zealand across all three formats and was initially signed as cover for Delano Potgieter, who was called up to South Africa A last month for their series against Bangladesh A.

He has featured in three Tests, two ODIs, and 18 IT20s for New Zealand, with Kuggeleijn playing first-class cricket for Northern Districts since 2014.

Hampshire are currently bottom of the Division One table with four matches remaining. After hosting Warwickshire, they travel to Nottinghamshire (September 8-11) and Leicestershire (September 15-18) before finishing their season at home to Sussex (September 24-27).

articles.title: Women's Champions Trophy: ICC confirm India as venue for inaugural edition after Sri Lanka removed from hosting rights
articles.summary: Australia, England, India, ​New Zealand, South Africa and Sri ​Lanka are the six teams that will ⁠compete in the inaugural ICC Women's Champions Trophy; Sri Lanka were originally announced hosts but have been replaced by India
articles.body:
The six-team tournament, taking place from February 14-28 next year, was due to be held in Sri Lanka but will now take place in the Indian cities of Mumbai and Vadodara.

Sri Lanka have lost the right to stage the tournament because of government interference in their board, with Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) currently holding an interim administration put in place by the Sri Lanka government.

The ICC said the SLC 'continue to make the requisite reforms' outlined at the ICC's Annual Conference in July, with Bangladesh and South Africa assessed as potential options before India were confirmed as host nation.

ICC Chairman, Mr. Jay Shah, said: "The ICC Women's Champions Trophy 2027 marks an exciting new chapter for women's cricket.

"As the inaugural edition of the tournament, it will bring together the best teams in the world in an intense, high-quality competition, while creating even greater incentive for teams to continue rising through the rankings and competing for a place on the global stage.

"With a marquee ICC women's event now taking place every year, we have a significant opportunity to build greater momentum, provide more consistency and create a stronger rhythm for the women's game, its players and its fans around the world."

Australia, England, India, New Zealand, South Africa and Sri Lanka are the six teams involved, based on their positions in the ICC Women's T20I Team Rankings on the July 6 qualification cut-off date.

All six teams will compete in a round-robin league, with the top two sides advancing to the final on February 28.

The matches ​will be held at the Cricket Club ​of India in Mumbai and Vadodara's International Cricket Stadium.

articles.title: County Championship: Henry Crocombe takes hat-tricks in successive games as 23 wickets fall in Surrey vs Yorkshire - round-up
articles.summary: Henry Crocombe takes second hat-trick in as many games for Sussex; Yorkshire and Surrey trade blows with the ball in action-packed day two that sees 23 wickets fall; Ben Stokes takes 3-40 but is bowled by wonder delivery from Yuzvendra Chahal
articles.body:
His sensational outing marked his third five-wicket haul in the County Championship this campaign, and just his second professional hat-trick after his first came against Somerset's tail in his side's last County Championship game.

Crocombe - who is set to sign for Surrey at the end of the season - finished the innings with an impressive 5-39, leaving his side with a first-innings lead of 102, which was extended to 188 by the end of play with Sussex 90-4 on day two.

Elsewhere, Surrey and Yorkshire traded blows with the ball in an incredible day two at the Oval that featured a staggering 23 wickets falling.

Jack White (3-14), Ben Coad (3-22), George Hill (2-17) and Matt Revis (2-19) led the charge for a Yorkshire bowling attack that skittled their opponents for 83, with only four players reaching double figures and Ollie Pope topping the Surrey scoring with a meek 21 off 44.

Yorkshire, though were subjected to their own skittling straight afterwards as they were bowled out for 82 having been 36-2, with Matt Fisher (6-25) dominating a batting lineup that featured just three players reaching double figures and notching just 46 runs for the final eight wickets.

Surrey - 27-0 in their second innings at close of play - need 158 to win to claim just their second County Championship win of the season.

Former England captain Ben Stokes was the victim of a wonder delivery by Northamptonshire spinner Yuzvendra Chahal on Thursday but responded with three wickets for Durham .

Chahal produced his best impression of the late Shane Warne's memorable 'Ball of the Century' in the 1993 Ashes when the former India bowler sent down a delivery which pitched outside off stump before it spun back dramatically to dismiss Stokes for 14.

Durham were all out for 205, but reduced hosts and Division Two promotion rivals Northamptonshire to 225-7 by the close of day two after Stokes (3-40) led his county's attack with an impressive performance.

articles.title: Smriti Mandhana: India's opener becomes all-time highest run scorer in women’s international cricket after record century
articles.summary: India opener Smriti Mandhana overtakes Mithali Raj as the record run scorer, across all formats, in women's international cricket; Mandhana also overtakes former Australia captain Meg Lanning for most centuries;
articles.body:
Mandhana smashed 124 runs from 64 deliveries to help India to a 137-run victory over Hong Kong in their second Group A match, as they posted 193-5 from their 20 overs before bowling out their opponents for 56.

The innings saw Mandhana reach 10,880 runs across all three formats for India and pass former captain Mithali Raj to become the all-time leading run-scorer in women's international cricket.

Mandhana's century - containing 14 fours and seven maximums - was her 18th across formats, which also saw her move past former Australia captain Meg Lanning for most centuries in women's international cricket.

"Until I was batting, I didn't know what record [I had broken] because I didn't know what exact runs [I had made]," Mandhana said in the post-match press conference.

"But looking back, I'd say a very good day for Indian cricket. Of course, Mithali [Raj] has been such a legend and a role model. We've all grown up watching her bat, so to go past in the tally of runs is something that I'd definitely not imagined to do."

She added: "Two of the legends of the game: Meg Lanning and Mithali Raj - these are the people I've grown up watching. I've tried to take a lot of things from them as batters, so really happy that I could go past them in whatever ways."

Mandhana made her India debut in 2013 and scored her maiden T20I century last year, becoming the first Indian batter to score a ton across all formats in women's cricket.

Raj, who held the previous record with 10,868 runs across formats, said on X: "Well deserved, @mandhana_smriti . I've watched you grow from a young player into one of the finest batters India has produced.

"To see you go past my record and become the highest run-scorer in international cricket is a moment I'm genuinely proud of. Here's to many more runs and milestones. Keep going!"

The 30-year-old could pass 11,000 runs during the Asia Cup, with India next in action against Pakistan on Saturday.

articles.title: England vs Ireland: Alice Capsey trial as wicketkeeper in keeping with England's push for 'world-class' all-rounders
articles.summary: As England finish international summer with 3-0 ODI series sweep of Ireland, national selector Lydia Greenway tells Sky Sports Cricket: "We don't want to be behind Australia all the time, we've got to close that gap. We know in the women's game, it's the all-rounders who dominate"
articles.body:
As part of that plan, all-rounders Dani Gibson and Freya Kemp have been starters throughout the summer, which included T20 series wins over New Zealand and India, as well as a run to the final of the T20 World Cup on home soil - before being beaten by Australia.

Charlotte Edwards' side were also well beaten by India in a historic first women's Test at Lord's, but they ended their summer on a high with a 3-0 ODI series sweep of Ireland.

"We don't want to be behind Australia all the time, we've got to close that gap," Greenway told Sky Sports Cricket during the third ODI win over Ireland on Sunday.

"And when you look at Australia, and how they're lined up in their top seven, they've probably got three or four bowling options - so we need to look at how we can do that.

"We know in the women's game, it's the all-rounders who dominate, and we have to look at that not just in the short term, but in the long term as well.

"If you're world class at your first skill, there's then wiggle room with what you offer in your other two skills. But I think if you are a very good international cricketer, but not world class, you have to offer us something else. That's my personal opinion on how we want to move things forward. I think that's really important."

For the ODI series against Ireland, England also trialled Alice Capsey at wicketkeeper, instead of regular starter Amy Jones - with the aim, again, being to add to the multi-faceted nature of their top order.

"With Alice Capsey, ideally, we would've given her this opportunity if it was a T20 series. That's where we see her potentially, if she can add that string to her bow," Greenway explained.

"She's proven herself a really capable middle-order batter, and by her having the opportunity to keep, if she has that role moving forwards, it frees up other spaces.

"It creates a bit more competition with Amy Jones, but she is very much the person who has the gloves at the moment."

What else did we learn from England series whitewash?

England wrapped up their international summer with a thumping 114-run win in the final ODI against Ireland in Worcester on Sunday, Sophia Dunkley starring with the bat as she cracked a run-a-ball 119 at the top of the order.

Reflecting on what the side will take away from the 3-0 series whitewash, former England bowler Tash Farrant told Sky Sports Cricket: "They've learnt that Sophia Dunkley's form has transferred into the 50-over format after a brilliant Hundred [tournament].

"Maia Boucher too, back at the top of the order, they could potentially be a good opening partnership going forward.

"They've also learnt that Tilly Corteen-Coleman is probably going to be in and around the team, playing with Sophie Ecclestone.

"Other than that, I would have liked to have seen Grace Potts, and maybe Charis Pavely get a game. I'm not quite sure I've learnt enough about the slightly newer players.

"They've won the series 3-0. That would have been first and foremost, but I still think there's quite a lot of questions going forward."

Greenway backs Sciver-Brunt as captain after Dean impresses

Former Ireland international Isobel Joyce also highlighted Charlie Dean's captaincy as a plus for England, having successfully led the side for the second time this summer in place of the rested Nat Sciver-Brunt.

"We already knew how good a leader she was, but they've now learned she's able to figure things out in the middle with new players," Joyce told Sky Sports Cricket.

"And, really important, she bowled well as a captain that was under pressure. She was able to take the bull by the horns when they needed a wicket, and bowled with real tenacity. That's what you want in any kind of leader.

"If you're Charlotte Edwards, who was a brilliant captain herself, game recognises game, and I think that's great for the head coach to see."

Despite Dean continuing to deputise impressively for Sciver-Brunt, national selector Greenway reiterated that the latter will continue to lead the side going forward and there wouldn't be a splitting of the role.

"Nat is very much our captain across all formats. I think she does an outstanding job," Greenway said. "She's one of the most unflappable characters that you can meet, and I think that's really crucial in that leadership position.

"In Charlie Dean and Dani Gibson, actually, I think what we've seen are leaders coming forwards who, if Nat does go down, then we know we've got options - and you could argue that we've never really had that before.

"Charlie Dean openly speaks about how she's constantly learning, and I've got a huge amount of confidence that, if Nat goes down again at any point, then she'll be more than ready to take over the reins."

articles.title: Kevin Pietersen: England appoint former captain as specialist mentor for white-ball teams
articles.summary: Kevin Pietersen will form part of England's coaching setup at the 2027 Cricket World Cup in October and November next year; the former Ashes and T20 World Cup winner said: "Putting on the England uniform again for the first time since 2014 is a profound honour and a deeply special moment"
articles.body:
Pietersen will join head coach Brendon McCullum's white-ball setup for the T20 international and ODI series' against Sri Lanka later this month, part of a coaching team that also includes Marcus Trescothick, Tim Southee, Jeetan Patel and Sarah Taylor.

The former England captain said of his appointment: "I'm immensely proud to have been asked to help this team on their journey to win a World Cup in South Africa.

"Putting on the England uniform again for the first time since 2014 is a profound honour and a deeply special moment.

"We have an incredibly talented white-ball squad, and I am excited to get in the trenches and work relentlessly hard with these players to maximise their potential.

"To be a part of Brendon's think tank over the next 12 months is a fantastic opportunity, and I cannot wait to get started."

McCullum said: "I've got immense respect for KP and what he's achieved in the game. He's had an amazing impact on English cricket, so for someone with his experience, knowledge and stature to want to play a role with this team is a fantastic result.

"I'm particularly excited for our batters to get the opportunity to work with him. KP has a unique understanding of what it takes to perform at the highest level, which will be hugely valuable to our players. We've always respected each other and had a strong appreciation for what the other brings to the game, so I'm really looking forward to working together."

Pietersen will be involved in England's winter's white-ball tours to Australia and South Africa, before joining up with the teams again for the home series against Pakistan and New Zealand next summer, as well as the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

The former Ashes and T20 World Cup winner played 136 ODIs and 37 T20 matches for England, scoring more than 5,500 runs, adding another 8,181 runs across his 104 Test match appearances.

Pietersen has previously worked as a mentor for Delhi Capitals during the 2025 Indian Premier League.

England fast bowler Jofra Archer, speaking on Monday ahead of England's third Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston, was in favour of the appointment.

"He's a legend of the game," Archer said "It will be great to have him around the group."

KP's history with England - good and bad - makes this a fascinating appointment

As Pietersen said himself in his statement, he's back donning the England uniform in a surprise move that I don't think many had seen coming, 12 years after his international career ended.

This, a player who once seemed a lost cause with regards to any potential reconciliation with the England hierarchy, and one who has been critical in the past of Brendon McCullum's 'Bazball' leadership, specifically.

But, though polarising he may be, there is no questioning Pietersen the cricketer in terms of pure talent. And England's next generation of white-ball stars are set to be the beneficiaries of his wisdom.

He was ahead of his time, playing the sort of extravagant, innovative cricket that is practically ever-present in the modern franchise era that was just starting to take hold during his career and somewhat accelerated its end.

His England career was never straightforward. He resigned as captain after only five months in 2008 following a breakdown in his relationship with then head coach Peter Moores, he was dropped during the 2012 Test series against South Africa series after sending text messages to the opposition, while dressing-room divisions during the 2013-14 Ashes as England were whitewashed 5-0 in Australia proved the final straw.

That history only serves to make this appointment all the more fascinating.

Trott appointed England Lions coach for Sri Lanka series

Jonathan Trott has been appointed head coach for England Lions' two-match T20 series against Sri Lanka this week, with a coaching staff of Troy Cooley, Graeme Swann, Ravi Bopara and Carl Hopkinson.

The England Lions selectors have selected a strong 20-player squad.

The extended squad includes seven players named in the England Men white-ball squads to play Sri Lanka later this month. Tom Banton, James Coles, Aneurin Donald, Will Jacks, Jamie Overton and Saqib Mahmood are included from the T20 squad, with Henry Crocombe drafted in from the ODI squad.

Former England batter most recently served as Afghanistan head coach, stepping down after the T20 World Cup earlier this year.

The 45-year-old has since taken up a short-term role with Ireland's men's side as a consultant for their series against his former employers.

He has made a notable impression in his relatively short coaching career, leading Afghanistan to the semi-finals of the 2024 T20 World Cup.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: 'Chickens come home to roost' for PCB as 'dismal' batting sees tourists bowled out within 34 overs in final Test
articles.summary: Pakistan's crisis-hit series against England worsened on day one of the third Test when they were bowled out for 133 within 34 overs; the third Test between England and Pakistan, at Edgbaston, continues live on Sky Sports on Thursday
articles.body:
"Unprecedented" was the word used by Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton to describe the upheaval that has occurred over the last week in response to heavy losses at Headingley and Lord's.

Seven players were sent home, head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul were replaced, and an investigation began into "media reports concerning discipline and conduct".

If those actions were aimed at provoking a response, the Pakistan Cricket Board did not get the one it would have been after on day one at Edgbaston.

On the eve of the third Test, Root dismissed suggestions that Pakistan have shown "no fight" in the series as disrespectful to both teams.

But after four hours of day one Josh Tongue (4-42), Ollie Robinson (3-15), and Jofra Archer (3-25) had cleaned them up with relative ease.

By over 10, Pakistan were four down with just 29 runs on the board. It took England 11 more overs to take three more wickets, Pakistan posting just 71 more runs by lunch with a dismal 110-7 on the board.

Things were wrapped up by the 34th over, a total of 133 all the visitors could muster on what was described in the Sky Sports commentary box as a "blameless" pitch. It has been a low-scoring summer, but this was low even by those standards.

But was any other outcome expected? Or was the display delivered actually the most likely amid an extremely testing set of circumstances.

"A thoroughly miserable batting performance from them," said Atherton.

"It is a batting line-up woefully low on confidence, " he later added.

"The decision to send seven players home - the chickens are coming home to roost. You cannot treat players like that and expect to build confidence in a side.

"Everybody who plays professional sport knows that if you play badly, the axe is going to fall.

"For all the criticism that has been made, just bear the context in mind that this Pakistan team looks dispirited - and there is a reason for that."

Pakistan's issues have been laid bare, and it is not going to be a quick fix. If they lose this, they will have one victory in their last seven Tests.

Couple that with the clear unrest and more upheaval seems almost inevitable.

"When I saw what happened, you could almost not see where the inspiration would come from - with the skill, the experience, and the alien conditions," said Sky Sports Cricket's Urooj Mumtaz.

"But to top all of it, the turbulent conditions and the manner in which [the changes were made to the side].

"Underwhelming, absolutely no competition, and this is the worst we've seen so far."

'Impossible' to play good cricket with off-field turmoil

So was it too big an ask of Pakistan to even muster up a semblance of fight?

Sky Sports Cricket's Stuart Broad said: "It looks like a really difficult environment to play in.

"You often talk about playing with freedom, playing without fear but the worst place you can be is feeling you need 20 or 30 runs to stay in the team - you never warm together as a group.

"It's really impossible to play good cricket when you have that many off-field problems going."

Pakistan find solace in debutant Razaullah

England ended day one with a narrow lead of 23 runs after losing four wickets. Two of them came from "bright spark" Razaullah (2-42), who provided Pakistan with some hope on his debut.

The 21-year-old hit speeds of over 90mph and took the key wicket of Joe Root to reinvigorate his team and show that the future of Pakistan cricket still has potential.

On day two, it will be about whether the youngster can continue his strong showing with ball in hand to make his side's poor batting performance count for as little as possible.

"Pakistan have been calling out for something different from their bowlers for a long while," said Sky Sports Cricket's Nasser Hussain.

"It is nice to watch that spell from Razaullah that had something, that had a point of difference, had some pace.

"It hurried one of the greatest batters there has ever been in Joe Root, and got him out."

articles.title: Joe Root's struggles and England century drought against Pakistan the only concerns from improved post-Bazball batting, says Nasser Hussain
articles.summary: England in complete control of third Test against Pakistan with tourists 268 runs behind at stumps; England dominate day two with the bat but Nasser Hussain highlights two areas for improvement
articles.body:
England piled on 453 runs to establish a commanding first-innings lead of 320 in the third Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston.

The hosts were firmly in control and on course for a 3-0 series sweep, with Pakistan closing on 52-2, still 268 runs adrift, when rain curtailed play.

"I've liked the tempo of the batting in this series," former England captain Hussain said.

"We talked about it earlier in the Bazball era, England going too hard and not seizing opportunities.

"They've got the tempo right, especially through the middle order with Harry Brook, Jamie Smith, Dan Lawrence and Gus Atkinson.

"I know it's a poor Pakistan bowling attack, but even Josh Tongue and Jofra Archer have contributed with the bat.

"I like Emilio Gay's tempo at the top of the order. He bats time and knows when to absorb pressure. English cricket, and this side in particular, have been crying out for that."

Despite the overwhelming positives, Hussain highlighted two areas England have yet to address during the Pakistan series.

Root's four dismissals have all been lbw, with the world's second-highest Test run-scorer continuing to wrestle with that mode of dismissal.

"Obviously, there are two boxes they haven't ticked," Hussain explained.

"Their greatest player is struggling with one specific type of dismissal: lbw.

"It's so obvious he's struggling. He tried to address it in the first innings, made a technical adjustment and then got out lbw again."

'England need to convert starts to big scores'

Meanwhile, England's wait for a hundred has reached historic levels.

Brook (75), Smith (69), Lawrence (65), Gay (60) and Ollie Robinson (50) have all reached fifty without kicking on to three figures.

A total of 14 half-centuries have been scored across the series without a single hundred, the first time that has happened in a Test series in England since the 1888 Ashes.

"The other one is getting hundreds," Hussain added.

"You can beat Pakistan with 40s, 50s and 60s. To beat Australia, or the New Zealand side we saw earlier in the summer, you need big hundreds and massive scores

"England just need to convert those starts into big scores."

Reflecting on the absence of a century in the Test series, former England bowler Stuart Broad has called for a reassessment of what constitutes a good score after a scorching summer has made conditions favourable for bowlers.

Broad argued that some scores this summer have been every bit as valuable as centuries on flatter pitches.

"Top-order batting has been very difficult in this series," Broad said.

"Root, England's best-ever player, has struggled for runs in this series. If he's struggling, it's OK for everyone else to struggle.

"We can't praise the likes of Ollie Robinson, who is getting 20-odd wickets at an average of around 6.00, and also say, 'We should be getting more centuries.'

"To be honest, this summer I think a 60 has felt like a hundred.

"You've had to work as hard for a 60 on these pitches as you would for a hundred on a normal Test match surface."

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Razaullah writes 'perfect chapter' to revive reeling Pakistan and force England into unwanted day four
articles.summary: Urooj Mumtaz lauded "a perfectly written first chapter" in Razaullah's Test career as he notched a stunning 81 off 63 balls on debut, smashing nine sixes; England set 130 to win on day four - watch live on Sky Sports Cricket from 10.15am, Saturday
articles.body:
Razaullah, who has only played eight previous first-class matches in his career, smacked nine sixes in his remarkable innings, equalling Tim Southee's record for the most maximums for a Test debutant, dazzling in a 121-run partnership with Mohammad Abbas (42) that eventually propelled Pakistan to a total of 449 and set England a target of 130.

The 21-year-old consolidated an already impressive performance on debut with the ball, taking four wickets in England's innings, including that of skipper Joe Root for his first.

His performance with the bat was undoubtedly the deciding factor in forcing the match into a fourth day that looked so improbable when he arrived at the crease, when Pakistan trailed by two runs at 318-8.

"His innings was simply sensational," Mumtaz said on Sky Sports. "A perfectly written first chapter of his Test career. All that passion, the flair of Pakistan cricket!

"One 21-year-old who wasn't even on the list gets on the plane and gets his baggy green. Then Joe Root is his first Test wicket, he takes a four-fer on debut, and makes 81, with nine sixes.

"All of Edgbaston and all of Pakistan were on their feet!"

'Razaullah showed the beauty of Pakistan's raw talent'

Mumtaz praised the spirit that Razaullah embodied, especially in the face of an off-field crisis that saw seven changes to the tourists' squad and a head coach axed ahead of the third Test after two heavy losses to begin the series.

"He showed the beauty of Pakistan and their raw talent - even he doesn't know what he's capable of!

"He's come off the plane and has absolutely no baggage. Yes he has a first-class hundred in dramatic fashion, but his hand speed is so quick he is ripping through the ball.

"He sits so deep in the crease and barely any of his boundaries are mishits - all of his sixes were monsters.

"That's the spark, the energy, the exuberance of youth that you are looking for.

"There was a smile on his face and he was not overwhelmed by the occasion. He didn't look in awe of it - he almost looked like he believed."

Razaullah: I just had to bat - you got to enjoy it!

Pakistan debutant Razaullah, using Urooj Mumtaz' translations after speaking to Sky Sports in Urdu:

"I just had to bat, you are the ones who get to enjoy it!

"I was planning to take it longer and deeper - 81 runs is not bad though!

"The ball was in my slot - I was eyeing that up and trying to provide support for the other batters and trying to take it as deep as possible - I broke both my bats and wore down my third.

"There was no point at which I didn't enjoy it or when I was scared.

"I was wanting the strike, and overall I wanted to keep the strike as long as possible to get Pakistan another day."

Mumtaz praised the role of fellow tail-ender Abbas - who notched his highest-ever Test score - in the partnership, and refused to rule out a miraculous comeback for Pakistan:

"To put one youngster in to bat with one stalwart of the game in Mohammed Abbas who is now on the honours board at Lord's after an eight-year gap between fifers," Mumtaz added.

"Abbas said 'I'm not just a seam bowler - I'm going to hit a few down the ground,' and he did!

"It all just amalgamates to show what could have happened if Pakistan had the temperament, the flair and the technique to back it up for the twelve-odd days of cricket we've had.

"If anyone is a betting person, after what's happened today, it's almost like that dimming light has been ignited again.

"You never know [what will happen]. Razaullah had a four-fer on debut [in England's first innings], and he provides a point of difference with pace.

"They'll have to believe - there will have to be words of wisdom - and also know that there's not too much to be said.

"They can leave it at that, watch some tapes and come back tomorrow with hope."

articles.title: England clinch Test series sweep of Pakistan: Joe Root and Jordan Cox steer hosts to eight-wicket win at Edgbaston
articles.summary: England secure first home series whitewash of Pakistan with eight-wicket victory in third Test at Edgbaston after Mohammad Abbas opened day four with wickets of Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay in first over; Joe Root - bowled off a no-ball - and Jordan Cox notch unbeaten fifties in win
articles.body:
The thought of England losing the Test match would have been unthinkable when Ollie Robinson reduced the visitors to 0-2 on the second evening - Pakistan still trailing by 320 at the time - but it looked a genuine possibility when the hosts themselves lost two in their first over to start the fourth morning.

Ben Duckett (0) signed off a miserable series by nicking off first ball to Mohammad Abbas (2-27), who added Emilio Gay (0) lbw to finish a stunning opener.

But any fears of England succumbing to a calamitous defeat were soon dispelled by their skipper as Joe Root (62no) struck a fine fifty, sharing an unbroken 128-run partnership with Jordan Cox (59no), who notched his third half-century late on, to secure victory in 24.2 overs.

Pakistan, meanwhile, will be left wondering would could have been, had Mohammad Ali not overstepped when bowling Root for 23 - dragging onto his stumps off a no-ball - with England just 35-2 at the time.

Will England stick with Cox for South Africa?

Cox's knock will have aided his hopes of retaining a spot in England's starting XI when the Test team are next in action for the three-match tour of South Africa, starting on December 17.

Jacob Bethell - injured for the Pakistan series - is expected to return to the side, but could he or Cox open the batting instead of Gay?

And were Gay to retain his place at the top of the order, Cox could yet fill in at wicketkeeper instead of Jamie Smith, who didn't keep during Pakistan's second innings due to an injured finger - though he has three months for that to sufficiently heal.

Pakistan were briefly hopeful of successfully defending a total of 130 or less in a Test match for the first time since 1993, when New Zealand were bowled out for 93, chasing 127, at Hamilton.

The last such instance of 130 or less being defended in England was when England set Australia 124 in the 1997 Ashes at The Oval and bowled them out for 104.

Pakistan unearth gem in Razaullah after series of struggles

In what has otherwise been a dismal series for Pakistan, they at least leave having shown some fight in this final Test by taking things into a fourth day and setting a target that briefly troubled England.

Also, in 21-year-old Razaullah, they have certainly unearthed a raw gem. The debutant knocked over England's all-time leading run-scorer Root in the first innings with just his fourth ball in Test cricket, on his way to a four-wicket haul, while his exploits with the bat on the third evening will live long in the memory.

When Pakistan's eighth second-innings wicket fell, they still trailed by two runs - England looking set to clinch their series sweep inside three days - before Razaullah proceeded to smash 81 off only 63 balls, clearing the ropes a staggering nine times to equal Tim Southee's record for a debutant.

Ultimately though, England are well deserving of the 3-0 series scoreline to herald Root's return as Test captain following Ben Stokes' international retirement earlier in the summer.

Root pleased with how England have dealt with 'chaos'

"The amount of uncertainty, noise and I guess chaos there was coming into the series, the way the guys have dealt with that - being so clinical with what we've had in front of us - and be stood here with a 3-0 win is really pleasing.

"We were clinical towards the back end there, a big partnership to see us home. It's exactly the sort of thing we're after and puts us in a nice place going into the winter.

"From 2-2, to be able to see that home with two guys set at the end, is a step forward in the right direction.

"The fact that everyone is contrubuting shows that they're good enough to perform at this level, which is a really good thing.

"We'll have different challenges in the winter and different surfaces, but can we keep taking strides forward as a group? Guys going on and making big contributions [hundred] will be one of them. That being said, we still made 400 twice in these testing conditions."

Butch: A lot of good things about England

"They were made to sweat for it at times, which is a good thing.

"It gave England pause for thought at times when it comes to differing conditions in Test matches - particularly with regards to South Africa and the ball not moving laterally as much.

"Perhaps a slight concern about the lack of centuries by the batters, but there was a lot of good things about England this Test match series.

"They weren't given much of a challenge for most of it, which is why yesterday was such a pleasing day as far as the summer is concerned."

Urooj: Major problems for Pakistan cricket

"There are problems with Pakistan cricket, major problems. They lost this series, drew in the West Indies, lost to Bangladesh at home, where their record isn't particularly good.

"They have now lost 11 out of 12 away from home and 15 out of the last 20 Test matches. Those are telling figures, as were the size of England's wins.

"Pakistan maybe had just one good day of cricket in the Test series. There are ingredients to work with but a lot needs to be done right for longer periods of time if there is to be a brighter Pakistan future."

Second Test (Lord's) - England won by 194 runs

Third Test (Edgbaston) - England won by eight wickets

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Joe Root says England are 'well placed' for South Africa series as series victory ends chaotic Test summer
articles.summary: England captain Joe Root says his side are "well placed" ahead of South Africa Test series in December; His side secured 3-0 series whitewash of Pakistan with eight-wicket win at Edgbaston; watch England face Sri Lanka in a T20I live on Sky Sports at 6:30pm Tuesday
articles.body:
Root (62no) and No 3 batter Jordan Cox (59no) put on a 128-run partnership that led England to an eight-wicket victory in the third Test at Edgbaston, bringing a positive end to a tumultuous summer that has seen a change in head coach, a new captain and numerous off-field issues make headlines.

The captain lauded his team's professionalism and work ethic and praised their ability in the face of outside noise on the way to their comprehensive series win.

"I think we're in a better place than we were, definitely," Root said. "Just having gone through [a tumultuous summer], I think you learn in chaos.

"You learn a lot about the group of players that you have, and for us to have come through this series as we have done, the way that we've gone about our cricket has been really pleasing, and as I say, [we want to] be a continuation of that now.

"In terms of everything that we've been through over the the last little while, for us to now be able to have the clarity and come through the other side of chaos, I think is a a really important part.

"You can only deal with what's in front of you, right? And once once everything unfolded how it did, it was how we responded to that, and that was the most important thing. And I think the group have done that brilliantly.

Root: Pakistan pushback was good for the group

A satisfied Root reflected on what turned into a challenging third Test for England after a heroic 81 off 63 from Pakistan youngster Razaullah on day three left England with a target to chase, claiming that Pakistan's resurgence will benefit his side in the long term:

"The fact that we've been able to start that journey and win a series in the manner that we have done has been really pleasing.

"We've had things go our way throughout the series. We had a little bit of pushback yesterday [from Pakistan] which, in a strange way, was quite a good thing for the group.

"Fair play to Razaullah, he made things difficult for us. He played some wonderful shots and made it very difficult to set fields to. He struck the ball nicely - I don't know how he didn't pull a muscle, swinging the bat that hard.

"But for us to come through that and be so convincing in the way we've finished the series - throughout the whole three games - has been really pleasing.

"We were clinical towards the back end there, a big partnership to see us home. It's exactly the sort of thing we're after and puts us in a nice place going into the winter."

'Runs were hard to come by - not just for us'

Concerns have been raised over the century-making ability of Root's side, with both England and Pakistan failing to register a single ton despite making 17 half-centuries across the three-Test series, marking the first trilateral Test series in England without a hundred since the 1888 Ashes.

Root, though, brushed off worries over his side's run-making, and praised his side's performance in challenging batting conditions.

"I think everyone would want to go on [and make a century] after getting yourself in, but it has also been the nature of the summer and the surfaces we've had - it has been across the board, not just necessarily us.

"The pleasing thing is, from 2-2 [after the first over if the second innings], to be able to see that home with [Root and Cox] set at the end is a step forward in the right direction.

"It would almost be more concerning if we were relying on just one or two individuals who were scoring hundreds consistently. The fact that everyone is contributing shows that they're good enough to perform at this level.

"We'll have different challenges in the winter and different surfaces, but can we keep taking strides forward as a group... that being one of them, guys going on and making those big contributions.

"That being said, we still made 400 twice in these conditions."

Second Test (Lord's) - England won by 194 runs

Third Test (Edgbaston) - England won by eight wickets

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Joe Root's best side in question ahead of South Africa tour and 2027 Ashes series
articles.summary: Sky Sports Cricket's pundits assess who stays and who goes with England's batting and bowling lineups yet to be decided ahead of a big 12 months; England tour South Africa before the 2027 Ashes; watch England vs Sri Lanka in a T20I on Tuesday live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
An eventful two months in English cricket has seen a the appointment of a new Test captain and head coach in Joe Root and Stephen Fleming amid a plethora of off-field issues that included multiple incidents involving alcohol and the retirement of previous captain Ben Stokes.

England's comprehensive series victory may have restored faith in a team who had previously lost seven of their last 10 Tests, but multiple questions relating to team personnel and leadership remain unanswered.

Here, the Sky Sports pundits assess the key dilemmas facing Root and Fleming...

Cox, Lawrence, Gay, Smith - who stays and who goes?

One of the most pressing issues facing England's selectors is that of the last remaining spot in an otherwise entrenched batting line-up.

Opener Emilio Gay, all-rounder Dan Lawrence, and wicketkeepers Jordan Cox and Jamie Smith have all featured in at least three of the summer's six Tests, but one of those four will have to drop out to facilitate the return of highly-rated Jacob Bethell, who has primarily featured as a No 3 for England.

Bethell has been tipped to open the batting in place of Gay - who has struggled after notching three half-centuries in six Tests this summer - while Cox has impressed both with the bat and in two days with the gloves after he replaced the injured Smith, notching a half-century in each of the three Tests against Pakistan.

"I would probably bring Bethell straight back in at three," Nasser Hussain said on the Sky Sports Cricket podcast. "You can't produce that hundred at Sydney the way he did and not have a Test match future.

"It's then Cox who looks vulnerable, or Gay - but I'm old school and think that opener is a specialist position.

"The two areas of English cricket we're looking for are a front-line spinner and opener.

"Gay has made a decent start, he looks like he could have a future but we're not certain. I would stick with him.

"The other option is you give Cox the gloves and axe Jamie Smith, but I also wouldn't do that. He's also done well with the gloves and got some runs."

Former England seamer Stuart Broad heaped on the praise for Jordan Cox after his composed 59no led England to victory in the third Test against Pakistan, adding: "I think Cox has done enough in this series to deserve a spot in the team.

"He's been composed, assured, calm, provided a match-winning innings today in a situation that was very difficult as a No 3 with England losing two wickets in the first over.

"That's the selector's biggest question - how do you get Cox in the team when Bethell is back.

"Huge credit to Cox for putting the selectors in that position - what I like about him is that he's got confidence in his own ability.

"One thing about this England team we've seen all summer is they lack a bit of leadership out on the field.

"I think Cox adds that. And I think he adds to the group and the leadership out there. I would have him in my XI come Pretoria in December."

The other area in discussion is England's bowling attack.

The four-pronged seam attack of Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue tore Pakistan's batting line-up to shreds for much of the series, restricting them to a score of under 200 in all of their first five innings and earning comparisons to the storied 2005 Ashes attack that interim head coach Marcus Trescothick called "fair" after the second Test.

Pakistan, though, were able to rebound on a flat Edgbaston pitch in their sixth innings, posting a score of 449 after a toiling day three performance that raised questions over whether England's bowlers were simply made to look good by favourable conditions.

Robinson in particular - who took a staggering 21 wickets at an average of 8.76 across the series - was questioned by Hussain, who identified his low speeds as a potential issue on more batter-friendly pitches.

"As we saw late yesterday - on England's one bad day - Robinson regressed to the mean, like the rest of the attack. His speeds were down and he was easier to play.

"He is what he is: he's a highly-skilled bowler, but if you keep him out there long enough, 78 mph becomes 74 mph - and that's a lot easier to face, even if it is nipping around a lot.

"You cannot argue though with his stats this summer. He's been absolutely fantastic with new-ball wickets up front. He sets the tone and wobbles it around - he's very difficult to play.

"Fleming, Root and whoever now just need to keep someone on his shoulder between now and South Africa, to make sure he rocks up fit for that first Test match."

Broad: We haven't learned a huge amount about Robinson

Broad, while complimentary of Robinson's success, feels the England seamer still has a lot to prove going into series against South Africa and Australia which will undoubtedly provide different challenges.

"Robinson looked relatively ineffective yesterday when it got a bit a bit flatter," Broad said on Sky Sports.

"Joe Root didn't trust him with the second new ball for more than two overs. But if he gets conditions where it nips around against this quality of batting unit, he's going to be highly effective.

"So I don't think we've learned a huge amount about Ollie Robinson. He's very good when conditions suit, but I expect the pitches to be different next summer.

"What I don't want to see is this trend of the keeper standing up to the stumps and the 75mph bowlers lobbing it up on a length continuing.

"At that level, you can have 25, 30 bowlers from county cricket that can do that job. On a normal Test match pitch, only five or six players can do that.

"Robinson has been given the ball in a summer that suited him, but there is no doubt that he delivered in an absolutely top-class way."

articles.title: England player ratings for third Test at Edgbaston: Dan Lawrence, Jordan Cox and Emilio Gay add to selection headache
articles.summary: Dan Lawrence earns Player of the Match honours at Edgbaston after hitting fifty, taking two wickets and claiming a stunning slip catch; Emilio Gay and Jordan Cox also hit half-centuries, with the trio tussling for a permanent place in the Test team as England sweep series against Pakistan
articles.body:
A Test match to forget for Duckett. In fact, it has been a pretty miserable series as a whole, with his first-innings 17 at Lord's serving as his highest score.

He did, however, notch England's only Test ton of the summer against New Zealand at Trent Bridge, so his place at the top of the order isn't under threat - at least for now...

He was also a bit butter-fingered in the slips this week, dropping three chances, albeit his two put down in the first innings didn't prove too costly as Pakistan were still bundled out for 133 in only 33.5 overs.

It has been a bit of a back-and-forth affair with regards to Gay's place in the starting Test side going forward, with the Durham left-hander seemingly locking up his spot with another battling half-century in the first innings - his third such score this summer.

But then his second-innings duck has somewhat opened up the debate again, especially given the performance of others who could end up elbowing him out of the way when the currently injured Jacob Bethell likely returns to the team.

It was, admittedly, a terrific delivery from Mohammad Abbas that ensured he wouldn't trouble the scorers in the second innings, but it's precisely why he'll be kicking himself with how he got out first time round - dragging a wide one from Razaullah back onto his stumps - when a first Test hundred was there for the taking.

Much like Gay, Cox's fortunes and future prospects see-sawed a touch over the course of this Test, as he copped a low one in the first innings - also falling foul of Abbas, lbw - but his calm, unbeaten half-century alongside the skipper on the fourth morning saw England to victory from a positon of peril at 2-2.

It will have been hard for Joe Root not to have taken note of that, as he looks for the right sort of characters to take this side forward. And Cox seems to have character in spades.

That was also evident with his keeping, when deputising impressively for Jamie Smith, who sat out the second innings with an injured thumb. He claimed four terrific catches and a stumping to finally end Razaullah's extraordinary knock.

Just when England needed a captain's innings, Root duly obliged, his unbeaten half-century on the fourth morning - just his third of a barren summer by his standards - allaying any fears of a catastrophic late collapse to defeat.

Instead, he celebrates a series sweep - England's first at home over Pakistan - on his return as permanent Test captain, though his lbw issues persist after Razaullah was the one to pin him in the first innings, in spectacular fashion with only his fourth ball in Test cricket. It takes Root's tally to eight such dismissals from his 10 Test innings' this summer.

Also, he moved one clear of Australia's Steve Smith and onto 220 in their personal battle to claim the record number of catches by an outfielder in Test cricket.

Brook will be another kicking himself for missing out on a hundred in the first innings, with one seemingly at his mercy before he needlessly ran himself out on the second morning.

He's been England's most consistent batter in the testing conditions served up this summer, with this his fifth half-century, while he has had starts of at least 20 in all but two of his innings.

It will make him all the more frustrated at the fact that a century has eluded him, but he has shown greater responsibility with the bat - certainly against Pakistan - which is encouraging after fans began growing tired of his, at times, reckless approach in the Bazball era.

Player of the match. With Ollie Robinson denied for the first time in a Test he's played this summer.

Lawrence is another vying for a regular place in this side and he's certainly done his chances no harm, with bat, ball and in the field.

His standout contribution was a spectacular catch in the slips - one-handed, diving low to his right - to see off Shan Masood five shy of a century. But he also grabbed two wickets in his 4.4 second-innings overs, including Azan Awais (59) to end his 125-run third-wicket stand with Masood and finally the wicket of Razaullah to end day three.

If anything his off-spin was under-used, with that being a key string to his bow to support England's preference for a four-pronged pace attack looking ahead to the winter tour of South Africa and next summer's Ashes.

With the bat, like Gay and Brook before him, he'll rue missing out on a first-innings ton when dragging a rather innocuous delivery from Mohammad Imran back onto his stumps.

The forgotten man in this Test, with his involvement ended two days in, as a blow to the finger when stood up to the stumps on day one prevented him from donning the gloves in the second innings.

It looks a precautionary measure more than anything, with it not keeping him from batting on day two as he again impressed with a typically brisk 69 before chipping one back to Razaullah off his own bowling.

While Cox impressed in his absence, Smith has also barely put a foot wrong behind the stumps all summer, so he'll likely still start if fit for South Africa.

It's been tough sledding for Atkinson this series, with only one wicket to show for his efforts prior to the second innings - as the rest of the pace quartet profited.

He has bowled better than his numbers would suggest, often coming on as second change, sidelined as others wreaked havoc with the new ball and when bowling to the tail.

But Root showed faith in his fast bowler after lunch on day three, with Pakistan 184-3 in their second innings, letting him loose for an eight-over spell that was his best yet and brought with it the wicket of Masood - as much as he owed a debt of gratitude to Lawrence too.

He'd later add Ghazi Ghori and Imran before he too couldn't escape punishment from the blade of Razaullah.

Robinson was at it yet again with the new ball, dismissing Saim Ayub and Abdullah Shafique in his opening spell in both innings, needing only four deliveries to see the back of them second time round - the former out for a pair upon his sudden, surprise call up to the touring side in between Tests that did him no favours.

Robinson's wicket of Saim in the first innings was his 100th in Test cricket, while his double strike in the first over of the second took his tally for the series to 21 at an average of 6.66 a pop, which grew to just the 8.76 apiece upon Pakistan's battling display on day three.

In all seriousness, his effectiveness does diminish when taken deep into later spells, which could be a concern on flatter decks if that's what awaits in South Africa or next year's Ashes, but it's extremely hard to pick fault given just how impressive his reintroduction to the side has been this summer.

Also pitched in with the bat, scoring his second Test fifty.

Not his best showing, with at least one of his three first-innings wickets a real gift from Masood, spooned straight to midwicket.

His dismissal of Saud Shakeel to a brute of a short ball in the second gave nod to him at his best, but he was one of several England bowlers to lose the plot late on the third evening as Razaullah smacked them to all parts.

Still, an encouraging summer on the whole, with five consecutive Tests for the previously injury-plagued pacer a real tick for England.

Trademark Tongue in the first innings, with three of his four wickets scattering the stumps - the top of Babar's off peg knocked back with the fast bowler's dream delivery, Imran undone by a toe-crushing yorker and Shakeel seen off by a devastating nip-backer.

He was expensive in the second innings, going at more than six an over, until his and Archer's bouncer theory proved incisive - until Razaullah arrived at the middle, that is - as Tongue got Babar to glove one behind.

articles.title: Australia's Steve Smith on 2027 Ashes series in England: 'I don't even know if I'll be there yet'
articles.summary: Steve Smith has a superb Test record in England - but will he still be around for Ashes series next summer? Australia batter laments dwindling role for spinners in Test cricket and says some wobble-seam deliveries are "just unplayable"; Australia face South Africa this autumn
articles.body:
Smith will turn 38 a couple of weeks before the first Test at Trent Bridge next June.

The batter has never won an Ashes series away from home and the 2027 contest would surely represent his last chance to do so.

Speaking to The Telegraph , Smith said: "I don't even know if I'll be there yet. I'm kind of a series-by-series proposition, as I've been for a while. That's still a fair way away for me right now.

"I'd love to win [an Ashes in England] but you wait and see if that comes to fruition."

Smith's Test record in England is stellar - an average of 54.27 across 23 matches with his haul of 2,334 runs including eight hundreds and 10 half-centuries.

The right-hander averaged a shade over 50 across his nine Test outings in 2025, while in three games this year - one against England and two versus Bangladesh - he is averaging 61.40.

He said: "I feel I'm batting really nicely. I've found different ways to go about things on these tricky surfaces and still be able to score runs.

"So trying to contribute as well as I can for the team, score runs, take catches, help out in leadership areas where I need to - it's been a good, fun couple of years."

Smith - who is eager to prolong his T20 career and play for Australia in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics - also had his say on how bowlers perfecting the wobble-seam delivery in Test cricket is making life incredibly difficult for batters.

He said: "There are some balls now that are just unplayable. Some of these balls have your name on it and you can't do anything about it.

"If it's seaming two degrees, you're not hitting that ball, or you shouldn't be hitting that ball. If you're hitting it, you're probably not a very good batter, to be honest. You're playing down the wrong line.

"And if it's coming into you, and it's hitting the top of the stumps and you're getting trapped in front, you can't do anything about it."

England did not play a frontline spinner during their recent 3-0 home sweep of Pakistan with part-time tweaker Dan Lawrence supporting the four-pronged pace attack of Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue, Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson.

For Australia, Nathan Lyon is not always a certain pick now due to seam-friendly conditions.

Smith added: "When the ball's moving as much as it is, and you can create relentless pressure by bowlers just continually hitting the spot, spin's by far the easiest thing to face and the thing that you can score freely off.

"It's a shame that we've had such spicy wickets that it's got to that point, because I love playing a spinner. I love watching spin bowlers bowl. I was a spin bowler myself back in the day.

"I'd love to see spin play much more of a part in Test cricket again."

Australia's next red-ball assignment is a three-match series in South Africa from October 9 - the first time they have tackled the Proteas away from home since the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 which led to bans for Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

articles.title: England coach Brendon McCullum wants Kevin Pietersen to 'challenge' him, has 'no problem' with previous criticisms
articles.summary: Brendon McCullum hopes Kevin Pietersen's "big personality" and "fierce competitiveness" can help England become best white-ball team in the world; KP now a mentor as side build for 2027 50-over World Cup; watch first T20 vs Sri Lanka live on Sky Sports from 6pm Tuesday (6.30pm first ball)
articles.body:
Pietersen will work with England for most series up to and including the 2027 World Cup, starting during the three T20s and as many ODIs at home to Sri Lanka this month.

The 46-year-old, who scored almost 14,000 runs across all three formats of international cricket between 2004 and 20144, accused England of a lack of preparation during a white-ball tour of India in 2025 in which they lost ODI and T20I series.

Speaking ahead of Tuesday's opening T20 in Southampton - live on Sky Sports from 6pm (6.30pm first ball) - McCullum said it was his decision to bring Pietersen onto the coaching staff and hopes his "big personality" will rub off onto the players.

The New Zealander told reporters: "When I rang him and asked whether he would be interested in coming and working with England, I think he thought I was joking for a start!

"He mentioned that he has been quite critical of us in the past and I said, 'I have no problem with that, mate'. There are parts I might agree with and parts I might not agree with and that's fine.

"The way he looks at the game is quite different to a lot of people and if someone can see something different and point that out to help you to become better, then I see that as no bad thing. Kev will do that and I have encouraged him to do that.

"I don't want him to be buried in one specific skillset - I want him to look across the set-up and challenge me privately on ways we can improve and do things differently."

McCullum continued: "The beauty of Kev coming in is that he has an incredible pedigree as a player - a lot of our players grew up watching and idolising him when he was in his pomp as a player.

"He is one of those guys where he has so much in his life so for him to give up those things to focus on trying to help us to get to the level we want and challenge for World Cups, we are incredibly lucky.

"Kev was an unbelievable player and a winner. He left no stone unturned with his preparation. He believed in himself in those big moments and more often than not performed in those moments. He is a big personality and fiercely competitive.

"They are attributes we would love to rub off onto our players. It is great to be able to add a resource like that and I only see an upside.

"He has brought a ton of energy to the set-up within the last 24 hours. His work ethic is second to none and when he is in on something, he is all in.

"I am super excited to have him, he is excited and the boys are buzzing."

Asked whether he had not been questioned enough by his other coaches, McCullum, 44, said: "That is the perception but the reality is that we are always challenging each other.

"I just wanted to add someone of Kev's stature as we look to become one of the best teams in T20 and one-day international cricket."

McCullum would not be drawn on whether success in this role could lead to Pietersen working with the Test team, saying reporters would have to ask incoming red-ball coach Stephen Fleming.

McCullum: We want our best players available across formats

Fleming replaced McCullum as England Test boss in August but did not oversee the 3-0 sweep of Pakistan, with Marcus Trescothick in interim charge for that resounding victory.

Fleming's first official assignment will be the three-Test series in South Africa over the Christmas period, although he has arrived in England from his native New Zealand for a flying visit that will include meeting Test captain Joe Root and chatting with the counties.

The former Chennai Super Kings head coach will link up with McCullum for the third and final T20 against Sri Lanka at Emirates Old Trafford at the weekend, where a big topic of discussion will be how the duo manage England's multi-format stars moving forward.

The 2027 50-over World Cup will take place a few months after the side aim to win an Ashes series for the first time in over a decade, with Harry Brook, Joe Root, Jofra Archer and Jacob Bethell among those set to be key in both tournaments.

McCullum added: "We have a big schedule with an Ashes and World Cup to aim for down the line but also big series coming up.

"We want to make sure we have access as often as possible to the best players across the formats and be aware of workloads as well. There is a bit to pick over but we will get there.

"The timing is perfect [for Fleming to be Test coach] and the team will respond to his style and his approach. He is a brilliant man, coach and tactician.

"He will do a brilliant job and I look forward to working collaboratively with him across the formats and getting the best for all three forms."

McCullum also confirmed that talks will be held over where assistant coach Trescothick now fits into the set-up.
